title: Sussex Pond Pudding
subtitle: Whole lemon inside a suet pastry case, with butter and sugar
excerpt: A suet-pastry shell encasing a whole pierced lemon surrounded by butter and sugar, steamed until the butter and sugar dissolve to a rich, tart sauce that pours out when the pudding is cut at the table.
sourceNotes: Sussex pond pudding is a traditional Sussex recipe, most famously described by Jane Grigson in English Food (1974). The whole-lemon technique is Grigson's defining contribution to popularising this dish. Earlier versions used currants in the butter-and-sugar filling without the lemon.

content.text: Sussex pond pudding is a suet-pastry case filled with butter, sugar, and a whole lemon, pierced all over so its juice seeps out during steaming. When the pudding is turned out and cut at the table, the sauce floods the plate in a buttery, bittersweet pool. The lemon softens completely over 3 to 3.5 hours until its skin is tender and its flesh almost dissolves. Use an unwaxed, thin-skinned lemon for the best result, a thick-skinned lemon will still be slightly chewy.

items.prepNote: unwaxed, thin-skinned, pierced all over with a skewer

content.text: Combine the flour and suet in a bowl with a pinch of salt. Add the milk a little at a time, mixing with a fork, until the dough comes together into a soft but not sticky ball, you may not need all the milk. Knead briefly just to bring it together. Cut off a quarter of the dough and set aside for the lid.

Grease a 1.2-litre pudding basin generously with butter. Roll the larger piece of dough into a circle big enough to line the basin, it should come to the rim. Press the dough evenly into the basin, working out any thin patches. The pastry should be roughly 1cm thick throughout.

Put half the butter cubes and half the demerara sugar into the lined basin. Press the whole pierced lemon into the centre. Pack the remaining butter and sugar around and on top of the lemon, filling every gap. The lemon should be completely surrounded.

Roll the reserved piece of dough into a circle to fit the top of the basin. Lay it over the filling and press the edges firmly to the top of the pastry lining to seal, pinch and crimp all the way around. Cover the top of the basin with a piece of baking paper and then foil, both pleated. Tie tightly with string around the rim and make a handle.

Lower the basin into a large pan of boiling water. The water should come halfway up the sides of the basin. Cover the pan tightly and steam over a medium-low heat for 3 to 3.5 hours. Check the water level every 40 minutes and top up with boiling water, the pan must not boil dry. The pudding is done when the pastry feels firm and has pulled away very slightly from the sides.

Lift the basin from the pan. Remove the coverings. Run a knife around the inside rim to loosen. Place a deep, warmed serving plate over the basin, deep is important, as the sauce flows freely. Invert in one confident motion. The pudding should release cleanly. Cut it at the table to reveal the lemon in the centre, and spoon the buttery sauce over each portion.

items.symptom: The sauce has not formed, the filling is solid butter and sugar
items.cause: The steam time was too short, or the heat was too low to keep a steady simmer.
items.fix: Return to the pan and steam for a further 30 minutes. The butter and sugar need consistent heat to melt and combine with the lemon juice.

items.symptom: The lemon skin is still tough and chewy
items.cause: A thick-skinned or waxed lemon was used, or the steam time was too short.
items.fix: Use an unwaxed thin-skinned lemon and steam for the full 3.5 hours. Thick-skinned lemons need 30 to 45 minutes longer than the recipe states.

items.symptom: The pastry has collapsed where the sauce pooled
items.cause: The pastry was rolled too thin in places.
items.fix: Aim for an even 1cm thickness throughout. Press out any thin patches when lining the basin. The pastry casing is structural, it must hold the sauce in.

content.text: Best eaten immediately. The sauce reabsorbs into the pastry as it cools and the pudding does not reheat well. This is a pudding to make and eat on the same occasion.
